Film star promotes Christopher Nolan film epic wearing gold artefacts dating back almost 3,000 years The Odyssey is a story about a Greek king’s long journey home. But a pair of earrings worn on the new film adaptation’s press tour – and their long separation from their homeland – is sparking controversy. At a photocall in London, Zendaya, who plays the goddess Athena in the Christopher Nolan film, wore a pair of earrings fashioned from Iranian artefacts dating back to 700BC. The backlash was swift, with archaeologists criticising the use of precious and culturally significant artefacts as accessories in the promotion of a Hollywood film, claiming it was a “hijacking” of Iran’s contributions to humanity.

Zendaya is under fire after wearing 3,000-year-old Iranian gold earrings at a London press event for The Odyssey. Jewelry dealer Barron London described the pieces as “a pair of Ziwiye gold medallion plaques, circa first millennium BC Iran.” Macquarie University archaeologist Peter Edwell said the earrings likely came from a “problematic hoard” that was “plundered” in the 1940s, not excavated. He noted the phrase “undisclosed origin” typically signals illegal looting tied to “criminal gangs and organized crime syndicates.” Islamic history expert Zirrar Ali called the choice “distasteful,” citing the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict, which has reportedly caused over 3,000 deaths. Barron London welcomed “informed dialogue about provenance.” The controversy follows separate criticism of Zendaya’s stylist Law Roach for using a private jet during the same press tour.

Prof Sussan Babaie, an Iranian-born art historian and Courtauld Institute professor, said it was “shocking to see that no one thought maybe this is not a good idea”. Expressing “outrage” that Zendaya was wearing the ancient objects, she said: “There is not enough cultural knowledge and cultural sensibility among those who dress [celebrities], those who accessorise them, those who put them up as the symbols of beauty and power and an expression of the movie’s high-mindedness.” Representatives for Zendaya and her stylist have been contacted for comment. The row comes amid scrutiny of western institutions that hold ancient artefacts. The British Museum has faced criticism over its looted Benin bronzes, sacred Ethiopian altar tablets and the Parthenon marbles.

Film star promotes Christopher Nolan film epic wearing gold artefacts dating back almost 3,000 years

The Odyssey is a story about a Greek king’s long journey home. But a pair of earrings worn on the new film adaptation’s press tour – and their long separation from their homeland – is sparking controversy.

At a photocall in London, Zendaya, who plays the goddess Athena in the Christopher Nolan film, wore a pair of earrings fashioned from Iranian artefacts dating back to 700BC.

The backlash was swift, with archaeologists criticising the use of precious and culturally significant artefacts as accessories in the promotion of a Hollywood film, claiming it was a “hijacking” of Iran’s contributions to humanity.

The earrings belong to Barron London, a Mayfair-based gallery and dealer whose website states: “With a reputation for discretion, the gallery works privately with collectors, estates and institutions to uncover and place pieces of significance.”

According to a formal statement from Barron, the artefacts, which were bought from another London jeweller, Glenn Spiro, in 2025, “are attributed to the Ziwiye hoard, discovered in north-western Iran in the late 1940s”.

The hoard was a trove of gold, silver, bronze and terracotta found in 1947 and looted by shepherds. According to a 2015 research paper, the surviving pieces were “sold in antique markets out of Iran in the 1960s” and “are now scattered in different museums and private collections”.

Prof Sussan Babaie, an Iranian-born art historian and Courtauld Institute professor, said it was “shocking to see that no one thought maybe this is not a good idea”.

Expressing “outrage” that Zendaya was wearing the ancient objects, she said: “There is not enough cultural knowledge and cultural sensibility among those who dress [celebrities], those who accessorise them, those who put them up as the symbols of beauty and power and an expression of the movie’s high-mindedness.” Representatives for Zendaya and her stylist have been contacted for comment.

The row comes amid scrutiny of western institutions that hold ancient artefacts. The British Museum has faced criticism over its looted Benin bronzes, sacred Ethiopian altar tablets and the Parthenon marbles.

payload.title: Zendayan muinaisesineistä tehdyt korvakorut herättivät arvostelua
payload.summary: Zendayan Lontoossa käyttämät korvakorut oli valmistettu lähes 3 000 vuotta vanhoista iranilaisista kultaesineistä. Asiantuntijat arvostelevat muinaisesineiden käyttöä elokuvan markkinoinnissa ja nostavat esiin niiden epäselvän alkuperän.
payload.content:
Näyttelijä Zendayan Lontoossa käyttämät kultakorvakorut ovat herättäneet voimakasta arvostelua, koska ne oli koottu lähes 3 000 vuotta vanhoista iranilaisista muinaisesineistä. Arkeologit ja taidehistorioitsijat pitävät kulttuurisesti merkittävien esineiden käyttöä Hollywood-elokuvan markkinoinnissa harkitsemattomana ja nostavat esiin korujen epäselvän alkuperän. Zendaya käytti koruja Lontoossa Christopher Nolanin Odysseia-elokuvan lehdistötilaisuudessa osana elokuvan markkinointikiertuetta. Hän näyttelee elokuvassa Athene-jumalatarta. Koruliike Barron London kuvaili osia Ziwiye-kultamedaljonkilaatoiksi, jotka ovat peräisin Iranista ensimmäiseltä vuosituhannelta ennen ajanlaskun alkua. Lähteiden mukaan esineet ajoittuvat noin vuoteen 700 eaa.

Alkuperään liittyy vakavia kysymyksiä

Macquarie-yliopiston arkeologi Peter Edwell arvioi, että esineet ovat todennäköisesti peräisin ”ongelmallisesta löydöstä”, joka ryöstettiin 1940-luvulla sen sijaan, että se olisi saatu talteen arkeologisissa kaivauksissa. Edwellin mukaan ilmaus ”alkuperää ei ilmoitettu” viittaa muinaisesineiden kaupassa tavallisesti laittomaan ryöstelyyn, johon voivat liittyä rikollisjoukot ja järjestäytyneet rikollisverkostot. Barron London ilmoitti pitävänsä tervetulleena asiantuntevaa keskustelua korujen alkuperästä. Arkeologien arvostelu kohdistui myös siihen, että arvokkaita kulttuuriesineitä käytettiin asusteina suuren Hollywood-tuotannon markkinoinnissa. Menettelyä kuvattiin Iranin ihmiskunnalle antaman kulttuurisen panoksen ”kaappaamiseksi”.

Valinnalta katsottiin puuttuneen kulttuurista herkkyyttä

Iranilaissyntyinen taidehistorioitsija ja Courtauld Instituten professori Sussan Babaie sanoi olevansa tyrmistynyt siitä, ettei kukaan ilmeisesti pysähtynyt arvioimaan valintaa. Hänen mukaansa julkisuuden henkilöitä pukevilta ja asustavilta tahoilta puuttui tilanteessa kulttuurista tietoa ja herkkyyttä. Islamilaisen historian asiantuntija Zirrar Ali puolestaan kutsui valintaa mauttomaksi ja liitti arvostelunsa käynnissä olevaan Yhdysvaltojen ja Iranin konfliktiin, jossa on lähteiden mukaan kuollut yli 3 000 ihmistä. Zendayan ja hänen stylistinsa Law Roachin edustajilta on pyydetty kommenttia, mutta vastauksia ei ollut kerrottu julkaisuhetkellä. Roachia on samalla lehdistökiertueella arvosteltu erikseen yksityiskoneen käytöstä. Korukiista liittyy laajempaan keskusteluun länsimaisten instituutioiden hallussa olevista muinaisesineistä: British Museumia on arvosteltu ryöstetyistä Beninin pronssiesineistä, pyhistä etiopialaisista alttaritauluista ja Parthenonin marmoriveistoksista.
summary_bullets: Zendaya käytti Lontoossa korvakoruja, jotka oli valmistettu lähes 3 000 vuotta vanhoista iranilaisista esineistä.
Arkeologi Peter Edwell arvioi esineiden olevan peräisin 1940-luvulla ryöstetystä löydöstä.
Taidehistorioitsija Sussan Babaie arvosteli valinnan kulttuurisen harkinnan ja herkkyyden puutetta.
payload.journalist_note: Esineiden ryöstämistä koskeva tieto on esitetty arkeologi Peter Edwellin arviona, ei varmistettuna omistushistoriana. Zendayan tai hänen stylistinsa kommenttia ei ollut saatavilla.

The backlash was swift, with archaeologists criticising the use of precious and culturally significant artefacts as accessories in the promotion of a Hollywood film, claiming it was a “hijacking” of Iran’s contributions to humanity.

Zendaya is under fire after wearing 3,000-year-old Iranian gold earrings at a London press event for The Odyssey. Jewelry dealer Barron London described the pieces as “a pair of Ziwiye gold medallion plaques, circa first millennium BC Iran.” Macquarie University archaeologist Peter Edwell said the earrings likely came from a “problematic hoard” that was “plundered” in the 1940s, not excavated. He noted the phrase “undisclosed origin” typically signals illegal looting tied to “criminal gangs and organized crime syndicates.” Islamic history expert Zirrar Ali called the choice “distasteful,” citing the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict, which has reportedly caused over 3,000 deaths. Barron London welcomed “informed dialogue about provenance.” The controversy follows separate criticism of Zendaya’s stylist Law Roach for using a private jet during the same press tour.

Prof Sussan Babaie, an Iranian-born art historian and Courtauld Institute professor, said it was “shocking to see that no one thought maybe this is not a good idea”. Expressing “outrage” that Zendaya was wearing the ancient objects, she said: “There is not enough cultural knowledge and cultural sensibility among those who dress [celebrities], those who accessorise them, those who put them up as the symbols of beauty and power and an expression of the movie’s high-mindedness.” Representatives for Zendaya and her stylist have been contacted for comment. The row comes amid scrutiny of western institutions that hold ancient artefacts. The British Museum has faced criticism over its looted Benin bronzes, sacred Ethiopian altar tablets and the Parthenon marbles.
